name: Long Beach
lede: Long Beach is a light yellowish tan from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary, and the single most common color matched in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: A dictionary tan, densely surrounded
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 *A Dictionary of Color* carries this tone on plate 12, B 4, first recorded there in 1922 [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS circular cites the same entry, naming it light yellowish brown, 4.5 units from Maerz and Paul's reading, notated 1.4Y 6.8/3.5 in the Munsell system [1].

It sits inside a dense cluster of tan and khaki neighbors: [[toupe]] and [[manila]] are each about 2.9 to 3.0 units away, almost indistinguishable, and [[putty]] and [[dust]] about 3.8 units off [2]. The name plausibly echoes the California city, but no source consulted here documents that connection, so it is left undocumented [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive matches this tone in 4,380 of 23,781 paintings, about 18.4 percent, the single highest share of any color, more common than 98 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks early, in the 1100s, present in 16.0 percent of the 50 paintings we have from that century, though that century's sample is thin [3].

Inside a painting it most often plays a light tone, in 44 percent of its 2,787 clearly-ranked appearances, a rank computed within each canvas so varnish cannot fake it [3]. Flemish still-life painter Cornelius Norbertus Gijsbrechts favors it most, in 10 of his 19 works here, 4.1 times his museums' baseline rate, and it is also most over-represented in Iranian paintings, 2.8 times the expected rate [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
